scenes.title: OVER()
scenes.narration: The OVER clause is the gateway to window functions, letting you compute aggregates and analytics across a set of related rows without collapsing them.

scenes.title: What OVER() Does
bullets: Defines a window: the set of rows a function operates over
PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups
ORDER BY sequences rows inside each partition
An optional frame narrows which rows count per calculation
scenes.narration: The OVER clause defines a window, which is the set of rows a function looks at. PARTITION BY splits the data into independent groups that are calculated separately. ORDER BY sequences the rows within each partition, which matters for running totals and ranking. An optional frame clause further narrows which rows are included for each calculation.

scenes.title: GROUP BY vs OVER()

left.title: GROUP BY
points: Collapses many rows into one per group
Returns one aggregated result per group

right.title: OVER()
points: Each row gains an aggregate or analytic value
Detail and summary live side by side

scenes.narration: The crucial difference is that GROUP BY collapses many rows into a single summary row per group, so you lose the individual detail. OVER keeps every original row intact while attaching an aggregate or analytic value to each one. That means you can see the raw detail and the summary side by side in the same result.

scenes.title: SUM() as a Window Function
scenes.code:
SELECT
  employee_id,
  department,
  salary,
  SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_total,
  salary * 100.0 / SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS pct_of_dept
FROM employees;
scenes.narration: Here we select each employee alongside a window aggregate. SUM of salary OVER PARTITION BY department computes the total salary for each department, but crucially every employee row remains in the output. Because we still have both the individual salary and the department total on the same row, we can easily compute each person's percentage of their department's payroll.

scenes.title: Adding ORDER BY for a Running Total
scenes.code:
SELECT
  order_date,
  amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM sales
ORDER BY order_date;
scenes.narration: When you add ORDER BY inside OVER, the window becomes cumulative. Here SUM of amount is calculated from the first row up to the current row, producing a running total that grows over time. The ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW clause is the frame, and it explicitly states that each calculation includes every row from the start through the current one.

scenes.title: How a Window Is Built
steps: PARTITION BY splits them into groups
ORDER BY sequences rows within each group
The frame selects rows relative to the current row
The function runs and attaches a value per row
scenes.narration: Conceptually the engine first takes the input rows, then partitions them into independent groups. Within each group it orders the rows and applies the frame to decide which neighbors are visible. Finally the window function runs and attaches its result to every individual row.

scenes.text: OVER() turns any aggregate into a window function that enriches rows instead of collapsing them — master it and ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LEAD, and LAG all follow the same pattern.
scenes.narration: Once you understand that OVER enriches rows rather than collapsing them, every window function follows the same predictable pattern.
